Take $U=\mathbb{Z}^2\subseteq\mathbf{R}^2$. Since $(0,0)\in U$, the set is nonempty. For any $(m,n),(p,q)\in U$, we have
\[
(m,n)+(p,q)=(m+p,n+q)\in\mathbb{Z}^2,
\]
because sums of integers are integers. Also,
\[
-(m,n)=(-m,-n)\in\mathbb{Z}^2,
\]
because negatives of integers are integers. Nevertheless, $(1,0)\in U$ but $(1/2,0)=(1/2)(1,0)\notin U$. Hence $U$ is not closed under scalar multiplication, so it is not a subspace of $\mathbf{R}^2$.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}
Let
\[
U=\mathbb{Z}^2\subseteq\mathbf{R}^2.
\]
The set is nonempty because $(0,0)\in U$. For $u=(m,n),v=(p,q)\in U$, both pairs have integer coordinates, and therefore
\[
u+v=(m+p,n+q)\in\mathbb{Z}^2=U.
\]
Likewise,
\[
-u=(-m,-n)\in\mathbb{Z}^2=U.
\]
Hence $U$ is closed under addition and additive inverses. On the other hand, $(1,0)\in U$, but for the real scalar $1/2$,
\[
\frac12(1,0)=\left(\frac12,0\right)\notin\mathbb{Z}^2.
\]
Thus $U$ fails closure under scalar multiplication, so it is not a subspace of $\mathbf{R}^2$.
\end{proof}
